title: Chapter 14
paragraphs: When Kitty had gone and Levin was left alone, he felt such restlessness without her, and such an impatient longing to get as quickly, as quickly as possible, to tomorrow morning, when he would see her again and be bound to her forever, that he was afraid, as of death, of the fourteen hours he had to get through without her. He had to be with someone he could talk to, so as not to be left alone, to kill the time. Stepan Arkadyevitch would have been the most congenial company, but he was going out, he said, to a _soirée_ — really to the ballet. Levin had time only to tell him he was happy, and that he loved him, and would never, never forget what he had done for him. The eyes and the smile of Stepan Arkadyevitch showed Levin that he took in that feeling fittingly.
"Oh, so it's not time to die just yet?" Stepan Arkadyevitch said, gripping Levin's hand with feeling.
"N-n-no!" Levin said.

Darya Alexandrovna too, as she said good-bye to him, gave him a sort of congratulation, saying, "How glad I am that you've met Kitty again! One must value old friends." Levin did not like those words of Darya Alexandrovna's. She could not understand how lofty and beyond her this all was, and she ought not to have dared to allude to it. Levin said good-bye to them, but, in order not to be left alone, attached himself to his brother.
"Where are you off to?"
"I'm going to a meeting."
"Well, I'll come along. May I?"
"What for? Yes, come on," said Sergey Ivanovitch, smiling. "What's gotten into you today?"

"Me? Happiness is what's the matter with me!" Levin said, letting down the window of the carriage they were riding in. "You don't mind? — it's so stifling. It's happiness that's the matter with me! Why is it you have never married?"
Sergey Ivanovitch smiled.
"I am very glad — she seems a nice gi...." Sergey Ivanovitch was beginning.

"Don't say it! Don't say it!" Levin shouted, gripping the collar of his fur coat with both hands and muffling him up in it. "'She's a nice girl' — such plain, modest words, so out of harmony with what I feel!"
Sergey Ivanovitch laughed outright with a merry laugh, which was rare with him. "Well, anyway, I may at least say that I'm very glad of it."

"You may do that tomorrow, tomorrow, and nothing more! Nothing, nothing — silence," said Levin, and once more muffling him up in his fur coat, he added: "I do like you so! Well, may I really be present at the meeting?"
"Of course you may."
"What are you discussing today?" Levin asked, never stopping smiling.

They arrived at the meeting. Levin heard the secretary hesitantly read the minutes, which he plainly did not understand himself; but Levin could see from the secretary's face what a good, nice, kind-hearted person he was. That was clear from his confusion and embarrassment as he read the minutes. Then the discussion began. They were arguing about the misappropriation of certain sums and the laying of certain pipes, and Sergey Ivanovitch was very cutting toward two members and said something at length with an air of triumph; another member, scribbling something on a scrap of paper, began timidly at first, but then answered him very viciously and delightfully. And then Sviazhsky (he was there too) said something as well, very handsomely and nobly. Levin listened to them and saw clearly that these missing sums and these pipes were nothing real, and that they were not really angry — they were all the nicest, kindest people, and everything was as cheerful and pleasant as possible among them. They were doing no harm to anyone and were all enjoying themselves. What struck Levin was that today he could see through all of them, and from tiny, almost imperceptible signs could read the soul of each one, and could see clearly that they were all good at heart. And Levin himself in particular they were all extremely fond of that day. That was plain from the way they spoke to him, from the friendly, affectionate looks even those he didn't know gave him.
"Well, did you like it?" Sergey Ivanovitch asked him.
"Very much. I never supposed it would be so interesting! Capital! Splendid!"

Sviazhsky came up to Levin and invited him to come round for tea. Levin could not for the life of him recall or grasp what it was he had disliked in Sviazhsky, what he had failed to find in him. He was a clever and wonderfully good-hearted man.

"Most delighted," he said, and asked after his wife and sister-in-law. And from a queer association of ideas — because in his imagination the idea of Sviazhsky's sister-in-law was linked with marriage — it occurred to him that there was no one to whom he could more fittingly speak of his happiness, and he was very glad to go and see them.

Sviazhsky asked him about the improvements on his estate, taking for granted, as he always did, that there could be no possibility of doing anything that hadn't already been done in Europe — and now this did not annoy Levin in the least. On the contrary, he felt that Sviazhsky was right, that the whole business was of little value, and he could see the wonderful gentleness and tact with which Sviazhsky avoided pressing his correct view fully. The ladies of the Sviazhsky household were particularly delightful. It seemed to Levin that they already knew everything about it and sympathized with him, saying nothing only out of delicacy. He stayed with them an hour, two, three, talking of all sorts of subjects but the one thing that filled his heart, and did not notice that he was boring them dreadfully and that it was long past their bedtime.

Sviazhsky walked him into the hall, yawning and wondering at the strange mood his friend was in. It was past one o'clock. Levin went back to his hotel and was dismayed at the thought that, all alone now with his impatience, he had ten more hours to get through. The servant whose turn it was to be up all night lit his candles and would have gone away, but Levin stopped him. This servant, Yegor, whom Levin had noticed before, struck him as a very intelligent, excellent, and above all good-hearted man.
"Well, Yegor, it's hard going without sleep, isn't it?"
"One has to put up with it! It's part of our work, you see. In a gentleman's house it's easier, but you make more here."
It turned out that Yegor had a family — three boys and a daughter, a seamstress, whom he was hoping to marry to a cashier in a saddler's shop.
Hearing this, Levin informed Yegor that, in his opinion, the great thing in marriage was love, and that with love one would always be happy, because happiness depends only on oneself.

Yegor listened carefully and obviously took in Levin's idea fully, but by way of agreeing with it he produced, much to Levin's surprise, the observation that when he had lived with good masters he had always been satisfied with his masters, and now was perfectly satisfied with his employer, though he was a Frenchman.
"Wonderfully good-hearted fellow!" Levin thought.
"But what about you yourself, Yegor — when you got married, did you love your wife?"
"Ay, why not?" answered Yegor.
And Levin saw that Yegor too was in an excited state and meant to pour out all his deepest feelings.
"My life, too, has been a remarkable one. From the time I was a child...." he was beginning, with flashing eyes, evidently catching Levin's enthusiasm just as people catch yawning.

But at that moment a bell rang. Yegor departed, and Levin was left alone. He had eaten next to nothing at dinner, had refused tea and supper at Sviazhsky's, but he was incapable of thinking about supper. He had not slept the night before, but he could not think about sleep either. His room was cold, but he was overcome by heat. He opened both panes of his window and sat down at the table opposite them. Above the snow-covered roofs you could make out a decorated cross with chains, and above it the rising triangle of Charles's Wain with the yellowish light of Capella. He gazed at the cross, then at the stars, drinking in the fresh freezing air that streamed evenly into the room, and followed, as in a dream, the images and memories that rose in his imagination. At four o'clock he heard footsteps in the passage and peeped out the door. It was Myaskin, the gambler he knew, coming back from the club. He walked gloomily, frowning and coughing. "Poor, unlucky fellow!" Levin thought, and tears came into his eyes from love and pity for this man. He would have spoken with him, and tried to comfort him, but remembering that he had nothing on but his shirt, he changed his mind and sat down again at the open pane to bathe in the cold air and gaze at the exquisite lines of the cross, silent but full of meaning for him, and at the rising lurid yellow star. By seven o'clock there were sounds of floor-polishers at work, and bells ringing somewhere in the servants' quarters, and Levin felt he was beginning to freeze. He shut the pane, washed, dressed, and went out into the street.
